canonicalName: Pythagorean number theory and musical ratios

milestones.label: Tradition credits Pythagoras with the concord ratios
milestones.description: Later tradition makes Pythagoras the discoverer that octave, fifth and fourth match 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3, though the evidence is indirect.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says Pythagoras noticed that string lengths in whole-number ratios give harmonious tones.
The correspondence is reflected in early Pythagorean sayings and so was probably known to Pythagoras, but the famous workshop story would not work.
The same entry doubts that Pythagoras himself was a mathematician or worked out the detailed mathematics.

milestones.note: Attribution to Pythagoras himself is disputed; sources are late. Dated by his floruit, not by any text.

milestones.label: Philolaus builds the cosmos on the concord ratios
milestones.work: Philolaus, fragments (esp. Fr. 6a), late 5th c. BC
milestones.description: The earliest surviving Pythagorean text to use the octave, fifth and fourth ratios as a structural principle is Philolaus' book, known only from fragments.

evidence.claim: Philolaus' conception of the cosmos centred on the match between the three concords and the ratios 2:1, 3:2, 4:3.
Philolaus, born about 470, taught the preceding generation of Pythagoreans before Archytas.
Standard modern study and edition of the fragments.
evidence.source: Huffman, Philolaus of Croton (Cambridge University Press, 1993)

milestones.note: Fragments are quoted by later authors, so the book has no publication year; the range is Philolaus' working life. Hippasus (experiment with bronze discs, reported by Aristoxenus) may be earlier; see notes.

milestones.label: Archytas: ratio theory and the four sciences
milestones.work: Archytas, Fr. 1 and testimonia (DK 47)
milestones.description: Archytas proved that no mean proportional lies between the numbers n and n+1, a number-theoretic fact behind musical ratios, and named arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music as sister sciences.

evidence.claim: He proved that superparticular ratios (n+1):n cannot be split by a mean proportional, and Fr. 1 is the earliest text naming the four sciences.
Standard modern edition and commentary.
evidence.source: Huffman, Archytas of Tarentum (Cambridge University Press, 2005)

milestones.label: Euclid proves the perfect-number rule
milestones.work: Euclid, Elements, Books VII-IX (IX.36), c. 300 BC
milestones.description: Euclid defines perfect numbers in Book VII and proves in IX.36 that 2^(k-1)(2^k-1) is perfect when 2^k-1 is prime, turning Pythagorean number lore into a theorem.

evidence.claim: The first known result on perfect numbers is Elements IX.36.
Definition VII.22 names perfect numbers and IX.36 gives the formation rule.
Primary text of IX.36 in translation.
evidence.source: D. E. Joyce, Euclid's Elements IX.36

milestones.note: Euclid's date is inferred (c. 300 BC).

milestones.label: Nicomachus' Introduction to Arithmetic
milestones.work: Nicomachus of Gerasa, Introduction to Arithmetic, c. 100 AD
milestones.description: Nicomachus gives the first stand-alone Pythagorean arithmetic: classes of numbers (perfect, abundant, deficient), figurate numbers and the link to musical ratios, stated without proofs.

evidence.claim: It was the first work to treat arithmetic apart from geometry and stayed the standard text for centuries.
Nicomachus classified numbers by perfect, superabundant and deficient, writing around 100 AD.
English translation by D'Ooge (1926).
evidence.source: Nicomachus, Introduction to Arithmetic (Open Library record)

milestones.note: MacTutor puts his life at about 60 to 120; the work is dated only by his floruit.

milestones.label: Mesopotamian tuning and ratio practice
milestones.description: Wikipedia reports that the fifth-based tuning later called Pythagorean already existed in ancient Mesopotamia, so musical ratios were probably used before the Greek theory.

evidence.claim: Pythagorean tuning is said to date back to ancient Mesopotamia and was misattributed to Pythagoras.

milestones.note: Wikipedia gives no dated tablet; searched Wikipedia and MacTutor only. Keep as an open lead, not a ranked date.

works.citation: Burkert, Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972)
works.whyItMatters: Standard critical account of the Pythagorean doctrines and their sources.

works.citation: Philolaus of Croton: his life and fragments (Huffman edition)
works.whyItMatters: Gives the earliest firm Pythagorean statements about concord ratios.
Edition and study of the surviving fragments, including the ratio theorem and the four sciences.

works.citation: Knorr, The Evolution of the Euclidean Elements (1975)
works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs how Euclid's Elements, including its arithmetic books, was compiled from earlier sources.
Standard late-antique arithmetic textbook, source of the later quadrivium.

notes: The split between legend and evidence is the main issue: Pythagoras left no writings, and modern scholars (Stanford Encyclopedia, Burkert) doubt the workshop story. Hippasus is reported (via Aristoxenus) to have tested the ratios with bronze discs. Euler's proof (18th century) that every even perfect number has Euclid's form belongs to a later event. Boethius' Latin arithmetic (c. 500, based on Nicomachus) carried this tradition to medieval Europe but is not listed as a milestone. No first_application is listed: the borrowing runs from music to arithmetic and no dated first use was found. Searched: SEP Pythagoreanism, Pythagoras, Archytas; MacTutor Pythagoras, Nicomachus, Perfect numbers; Wikipedia Pythagorean tuning, Perfect number, Nicomachus.

phases: Callippus' 34 spheres and Aristotle's physical spheres

milestones.label: Academy programme of uniform circular motion
milestones.description: Eudoxus worked in Plato's circle, where heavenly motion was expected to be simple and regular; this is the setting, not a dated text.

evidence.claim: Eudoxus is believed to have been influenced by Plato and Pythagoras when he designed the spheres.
Eudoxus fits the Pythagorean and Platonic ideal of simplicity; a cited article argues the inspiration was Pythagorean, not Platonic.

milestones.note: Dating is by the period of Eudoxus' Academy contacts. MacTutor records a dispute over whether Plato or the Pythagoreans inspired the model.

milestones.label: Eudoxus proposes the homocentric spheres
milestones.work: Eudoxus, On Speeds (lost), c. 370-355 BC
milestones.description: Eudoxus explained planetary paths, including retrogression, by nested spheres all centred on the Earth; his book is lost and the system is known through Aristotle and Simplicius.

evidence.claim: Eudoxus built a system of rotating spheres to account for the heavenly motions; the work On Speeds is lost.
The model had 27 spheres; our knowledge comes from Aristotle and Simplicius.
Aristotle describes Eudoxus' spheres for sun, moon and planets.

milestones.note: Eudoxus lived 408-355 BC (MacTutor). The treatise is lost, so the date is a range from his life; the earliest surviving report is Aristotle's.

milestones.label: Aristotle turns the spheres into a physical cosmos
milestones.work: Aristotle, Metaphysics XII.8 and On the Heavens
milestones.description: Aristotle added unrolling spheres between the planetary sets and treated them as real bodies, giving 55 (or 47) spheres.

evidence.claim: Aristotle accepted the theory as physically real, not just a mathematical model.
He added to Callippus' system for a total of fifty-five spheres and later doubted the count.
Technical study of Aristotle's corrections.

milestones.note: Aristotle died in 322 BC.

milestones.label: Callippus tests the spheres against observed seasons
milestones.work: Callippus, adjustments reported in Aristotle, Metaphysics XII.8
milestones.description: Callippus found 27 spheres too few, added seven, and tied the scheme to measured season lengths and a 76-year cycle starting in 330 BC.

evidence.claim: He added two spheres each for sun and moon and one each for Mercury, Venus, Mars, and measured the seasons.
He worked with Aristotle from 330 BC, correcting and completing Eudoxus' discoveries; his cycle began in 330 BC.
Aristotle reports Callippus' extra spheres.

milestones.note: Treated as first_application because it is the first recorded fit of the spheres to observation; Eudoxus' own use of data is doubted (MacTutor quotes Neugebauer).

milestones.label: Schiaparelli reconstructs the spheres
milestones.work: Schiaparelli, Le sfere omocentriche di Eudosso, di Callippo e di Aristotele (Milan, 1875)
milestones.description: Schiaparelli's geometric reconstruction of the figure-eight hippopede made the lost system understandable and set the later debate.

evidence.claim: Scanned record of the 1875 book.
Modern reconstructions of the planetary model follow Schiaparelli's.
Later technical studies of the hippopede and the geometry.
evidence.source: Yavetz, On the homocentric spheres of Eudoxus, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 52 (1998)

milestones.label: Schiaparelli titles the spheres as homocentric
milestones.work: Schiaparelli, G. V., Le sfere omocentriche di Eudosso, di Callippo e di Aristotele, 1875
milestones.description: The earliest title found that uses the homocentric-spheres name (Italian form).

evidence.claim: zbMATH record gives the title with year 1875 (Brera series)
Open Library lists the same title with first publication year 1874

milestones.note: Records disagree: zbMATH 1875 (kept, matches the existing record) vs Open Library 1874. Not checked against a physical copy.

works.citation: On Speeds (lost); reconstructions: Riddell, Eudoxan mathematics and the Eudoxan spheres, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 20
works.whyItMatters: Modern study of the geometry of the spheres.

works.citation: Aristotle, Metaphysics, trans. W. D. Ross (Oxford, 1924)
works.whyItMatters: Standard English text of Aristotle's account of the sphere system in Metaphysics XII.

works.citation: Le sfere omocentriche di Eudosso, di Callippo e di Aristotele
works.whyItMatters: Classic reconstruction of the system.

notes: Eudoxus' own text is lost, so no first_statement year can be tied to a publication. Some scholars doubt that his model could be matched to numerical data (MacTutor quotes Neugebauer). Mendell (1998) discusses Callippus' curves (DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0498.1998.tb00534.x). The homocentric tradition was displaced by epicycle and eccentric models (Apollonius, Hipparchus, Ptolemy). No naming or institution milestone was found, so the institutional date is null. Autolycus' On the Moving Sphere (c. 330 BC, MacTutor Greek astronomy) is related spherical geometry. Searched: MacTutor Eudoxus, Callippus, Greek astronomy; Wikipedia Concentric spheres, Callippus, Eudoxus; Perseus Metaphysics XII.8. person without verified work: Callippus of Cyzicus (developer). Re-checked the MacTutor Eudoxus page in this pass: it gives no date for an Academy programme in 387 BC and no Plato-Pythagorean motive; the -387 and motive stay interpretive and unresolved.

canonicalName: Eudoxus: theory of proportion and method of exhaustion

milestones.label: Discovery of incommensurable magnitudes
milestones.description: The Pythagoreans are credited with finding irrational ratios, which made a new theory of ratio necessary.

evidence.claim: The discovery of irrationals is attributed to the Pythagoreans, though probably not to Pythagoras.
Standard study of the Elements' theory of incommensurables.
evidence.source: Knorr, The Evolution of the Euclidean Elements (1975)

milestones.note: Date and discoverer are uncertain; shown only as background.

milestones.label: Antiphon's inscribed polygons
milestones.description: Antiphon doubled the sides of a polygon inscribed in a circle, the first recorded step toward exhausting a curved area.

evidence.claim: Antiphon inscribed a square, then 8-gon, 16-gon and so on; his methods contained ideas leading to integration.
The exhaustion idea began with Antiphon in the late 5th century BC.

milestones.label: Eudoxus' definition of equal ratios
milestones.work: Eudoxus' lost theory, preserved as Euclid, Elements V
milestones.description: Eudoxus compared ratios of any magnitudes, rational or not, by comparing multiples, which handled incommensurables.

evidence.claim: He made a definition allowing possibly irrational lengths to be compared; his works are lost.
Eudoxus was probably the source for most of Euclid's Book V.

milestones.note: Known only through Euclid V and Archimedes; the range is from Eudoxus' life (408-355 BC).

milestones.label: Eudoxus proves the cone and pyramid volumes by exhaustion
milestones.work: Eudoxus' proofs, as reported by Archimedes
milestones.description: Democritus had stated that cone and pyramid are one third of cylinder and prism; Eudoxus supplied the first proof using exhaustion.

evidence.claim: Heath's introduction says Eudoxus first proved these results scientifically, while Democritus first asserted them.
evidence.source: Heath, The Method of Archimedes (1912), introduction

evidence.claim: Eudoxus made Antiphon's idea rigorous, proving the one-third results later credited to him by Archimedes.

milestones.note: Same date range as first_statement; order within it is unknown.

milestones.label: Euclid's Elements V and XII
milestones.work: Euclid, Elements, Books V and XII
milestones.description: Euclid gathers Eudoxus' theory of proportion in Book V and uses exhaustion to prove area and volume results in Book XII.

evidence.claim: Proclus says Euclid collected many of Eudoxus' theorems; Book V is probably Eudoxan.
Euclid uses exhaustion for six propositions in Book XII.
Primary text of the definition of equal ratios.
evidence.source: D. E. Joyce, Elements V, definition 5

evidence.claim: Primary text of XII.2, circles are as squares on diameters.

milestones.note: Euclid's date is inferred (c. 300 BC).

milestones.label: Archimedes applies exhaustion widely
milestones.work: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola, Measurement of a Circle, On the Sphere and Cylinder
milestones.description: Archimedes states the lemma now named after him and uses exhaustion for the parabola, circle, sphere and spiral.

evidence.claim: He used exhaustion to obtain a wide range of results.
Quadrature of the Parabola states the lemma used by Eudoxus and earlier mathematicians.

milestones.note: Archimedes lived 287-212 BC; the individual treatises are not securely dated.

milestones.label: The name 'method of exhaustion'
milestones.work: Gregorius a Sancto Vincentio, Opus geometricum quadraturae circuli et sectionum coni (Antwerp, 1647)
milestones.description: The term exhaustion for the method is credited to Saint-Vincent, who wrote that a quantity is exhausted.

evidence.claim: The first use of the term was in 1647 by Gregory of Saint Vincent.
MacTutor quotes his phrase about a quantity being exhausted and dates the Opus geometricum to 1647.
Scanned copy of the 1647 book.

milestones.note: Priority for the exact coinage rests on Wikipedia; MacTutor confirms only the book and the idea.

milestones.label: Dedekind's real numbers and Eudoxus' ratios
milestones.work: Dedekind, Stetigkeit und irrationale Zahlen (1872)
milestones.description: Dedekind's cuts are often compared with Eudoxus' definition, though whether Eudoxus influenced him is disputed.

evidence.claim: Eudoxus' work inspired Dedekind's work on real numbers.
MacTutor reports a view that Dedekind's definition was radically original and not influenced by Eudoxus.
Stein's comparison of the two theories.
Open Library record of the 1872 booklet.

milestones.note: Influence is contested; the milestone records the later reception, not a proven line.

works.citation: Knorr, The Evolution of the Euclidean Elements (1975)
works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs how Euclid's Elements, including its arithmetic books, was compiled from earlier sources.

works.citation: Knorr, The Evolution of the Euclidean Elements (1975)
works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs how Euclid's Elements, including its arithmetic books, was compiled from earlier sources.
Reconstructs the palimpsest that preserves Archimedes' Method, the source of his mechanical procedure.
Source of the term and an early step toward limits.
Modern analogue of Eudoxus' definition.

notes: No text by Eudoxus survives; both parts of the theory rest on Euclid, Archimedes and later testimony, so first_statement and first_application share one date range. Archimedes attributes the cone and pyramid proofs to Eudoxus. Antiphon and Bryson (circumscribed polygons) are earlier steps. Dedekind influence is disputed (Corry 1994 and Stein 1990 are discussed in MacTutor). Searched: MacTutor Eudoxus, Squaring the circle, Saint-Vincent; Wikipedia Method of exhaustion, Eudoxus, Euclid's Elements; Heath 1912 (Internet Archive); Joyce's Elements. person without verified work: Antiphon (originator).

canonicalName: Euclid's Elements, Books VII-IX: arithmetic as a deductive theory

milestones.label: Pythagorean odd and even arithmetic
milestones.description: Fifth-century Pythagoreans handled odd and even numbers; van der Waerden suggests Book VII draws on a Pythagorean textbook, and the Euclidean algorithm may predate Euclid.

evidence.claim: Numbers and the odd and the even play a prominent role in Philolaus (Frs. 4-5).
Van der Waerden suggests Book VII derives from a Pythagorean number-theory textbook; the algorithm was probably known to Eudoxus around 375 BC.

milestones.note: Hypothesis about a lost textbook; no surviving text.

milestones.label: Archytas proves a ratio theorem for numbers
milestones.work: Archytas, as reported by Boethius and used in the Sectio canonis
milestones.description: Archytas showed that no number lies in proportion between n and n+1, an early proof about integers.

evidence.claim: He proved ratios (n+1):n cannot be divided by a mean proportional.

milestones.label: Euclid, Elements VII-IX
milestones.work: Euclid, Elements, Books VII-IX, c. 300 BC
milestones.description: Euclid presents divisibility, the Euclidean algorithm, primes, geometric progressions of integers, infinitely many primes (IX.20) and even perfect numbers (IX.36) as a deductive body.

evidence.claim: Books 7-9 deal with number theory; Book 7 is a self-contained introduction containing the Euclidean algorithm.
Book IX contains the infinitude of primes, the geometric-series sum and the perfect-number construction.
Primary text of Book VII (definitions and the algorithm).
evidence.source: D. E. Joyce, Elements Book VII

evidence.claim: Interpretive study of the arithmetic books.
evidence.source: Knorr, Problems in the interpretation of Greek number theory, Stud. Hist. Philos. Sci. 7 (1976)

milestones.note: Euclid's date is inferred (c. 300 BC; MacTutor gives birth about 325 BC).

milestones.label: Euclid's Elements as the first deductive arithmetic
milestones.work: Euclid, Elements, Books VII-IX
milestones.description: The same books are also the first surviving systematic treatment, so they serve as the field's founding textbook.

evidence.claim: The Elements is the oldest extant large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics.

milestones.note: Same work as the first_statement; listed twice because it is both the earliest surviving statement and the first systematic treatment.

milestones.label: Nicomachus' stand-alone arithmetic
milestones.work: Nicomachus, Introduction to Arithmetic, c. 100 AD
milestones.description: Nicomachus writes the first book treating arithmetic apart from geometry, without proofs.

evidence.claim: It was the first work to treat arithmetic as a separate topic from geometry.
Open Library record of the translation.

milestones.label: First printed Elements
milestones.work: Euclid, Elements, ed. Erhard Ratdolt (Venice, 1482)
milestones.description: The first printed edition spread Euclid's arithmetic books through Europe.

evidence.claim: The first printed edition was published by Erhard Ratdolt in 1482.

milestones.label: Euler proves the converse of Euclid's perfect-number rule
milestones.work: Euler, work on even perfect numbers (18th century)
milestones.description: Euler showed that every even perfect number has Euclid's form, completing IX.36.

evidence.claim: Euler proved in the 18th century that the formula yields all even perfect numbers; Alhazen had conjectured it earlier.

milestones.note: The exact paper and year were not verified; only the century is stated by the source.

works.citation: Knorr, The Evolution of the Euclidean Elements (1975)
works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs how Euclid's Elements, including its arithmetic books, was compiled from earlier sources.
Contains the ratio theorem used later in Euclid-style number theory.

works.citation: Knorr, The Evolution of the Euclidean Elements (1975)
works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs how Euclid's Elements, including its arithmetic books, was compiled from earlier sources.
Stand-alone arithmetic text built on this tradition.

notes: Euclid probably compiled earlier material (Proclus, Wikipedia); the Pythagorean-textbook origin of Book VII is a hypothesis of van der Waerden. The Euclidean algorithm also appears in Book X (lengths). Knorr (1976) argues about whether Euclid has a fundamental theorem of arithmetic. Euler's lifespan is quoted from general knowledge and was not checked against a fetched source. Searched: MacTutor Euclid, Nicomachus, Perfect numbers; Wikipedia Euclid's Elements, Euclidean algorithm, Euclid-Euler theorem. person without verified work: Leonhard Euler (developer).

milestones.label: Pingala's Chandahshastra
milestones.work: Pingala, Chandahshastra (Chandas Sutra), c. 3rd-2nd c. BCE
milestones.description: Pingala gives rules to list, index and count all metres built from short and long syllables, which amounts to enumerating binary sequences and binomial counts.

evidence.claim: The text gives prastara, nashta, uddishta and related procedures and a triangular array of binomial coefficients.
Dated to the final centuries BCE; the exact date is uncertain.
Modern study of Indian metrical combinatorics and the Fibonacci link.
evidence.source: Singh, The so-called Fibonacci numbers in ancient and medieval India, Historia Math. 12 (1985)

milestones.note: Wikipedia's Virahanka page dates Pingala to the 4th century BCE, his own page to the 3rd or 2nd; the range follows the latter. Claims of binary notation and an early zero are modern interpretations.

milestones.label: Virahanka's Fibonacci-type counts
milestones.work: Virahanka, work on prosody (6th-8th c. AD)
milestones.description: Virahanka counts metres of a given total length where long syllables count two beats, giving the Fibonacci recurrence.

evidence.claim: He was an Indian prosodist, 6th to 8th century, building on Pingala, regarded as first to propose the Fibonacci sequence.
Singh's survey traces Virahanka, Gopala and Hemachandra.

milestones.label: Halayudha's staircase of Mount Meru
milestones.work: Halayudha, Mritasanjivani (commentary on Chandahshastra), 10th c.
milestones.description: Halayudha explains Pingala's rules with the meru-prastara, a triangular array equivalent to Pascal's triangle, and also names it.

evidence.claim: His method of pyramidal expansion (meru-prastara) is equivalent to Pascal's triangle; he lived in the 10th century.
Same attribution in the history of the triangle.
Jaina commentary of the 10th century also shows the triangle.

milestones.note: Both the explicit triangle and its Sanskrit name appear here; one milestone covers both.

milestones.label: Pascal's Treatise on the Arithmetical Triangle
milestones.work: Pascal, Traite du triangle arithmetique (written 1654, published 1665)
milestones.description: Pascal collected the properties of the triangle and used them for probability, giving the first systematic European treatment.

evidence.claim: Published posthumously in 1665; Pascal collected known results and applied them to probability.
Open Library record.

milestones.label: The triangle is named after Pascal
milestones.work: Montmort, Essay d'analyse sur les jeux de hazard (1708)
milestones.description: Montmort called it Pascal's table for combinations, followed by de Moivre in 1730, giving the Western name.

evidence.claim: Named for Pascal by Montmort (1708) and de Moivre (1730).

milestones.note: Names the triangle, not the field; the Indian lineage keeps its own names.

milestones.label: First Western edition of the Chandahshastra
milestones.work: A. Weber, Indische Studien 8 (Leipzig, 1863)
milestones.description: Weber's edition brought Pingala's text to Western scholars.

evidence.claim: Weber's edition is the earliest listed in Wikipedia's editions of the text.

milestones.note: Volume number comes from Wikipedia; not verified in a library record.

works.whyItMatters: Modern study of the syllable-counting rules behind the early combinatorial patterns.

works.citation: Prosody work discussed in Singh, Historia Math. 12
works.whyItMatters: Earliest known Fibonacci-type recurrence in the tradition.

works.citation: Singh survey of Indian Fibonacci numbers
works.whyItMatters: Records his later treatment of the same sequence.
Brought the triangle into probability and European mathematics.
First Western edition.

notes: No first_application is listed: the counting rules are used inside prosody, and no dated first use outside it was found. Dating of Pingala varies by source (4th century BCE vs 3rd-2nd). Jaina texts (Bhagabati Sutra, about 300 BC) give permutation and combination rules independently (MacTutor). The triangle also appears in Persia (al-Karaji), China (Jia Xian, Yang Hui) and Europe (Apian 1527, Stifel 1544, Tartaglia 1556) per Wikipedia. Weber's lifespan is from general knowledge, not a fetched source. Searched: Wikipedia Pingala, Halayudha, Virahanka, Hemachandra, Pascal's triangle; MacTutor Indian and Jaina mathematics; Singh 1985 (Crossref, zbMATH). person without verified work: Halayudha (systematiser). Re-checked Wikipedia Pingala in this pass: it gives c. 3rd to 2nd century BCE, so the -300 milestone sits inside that range and a 4th-century date is not supported.

canonicalName: Archimedes' mechanical method for areas and volumes
aliases: law of the lever in geometry
phases: Lever law and centres of gravity

milestones.label: Democritus asserts the cone and pyramid volumes
milestones.description: Democritus first stated that cone and pyramid are one third of cylinder and prism, a result Archimedes says he discovered by his method.

evidence.claim: Democritus was first to assert these volumes; Eudoxus first proved them.
evidence.source: Heath, The Method of Archimedes (1912), introduction

milestones.note: Dated by Democritus' working life; the argument is a reconstruction.

milestones.label: Quadrature of the Parabola outlines the mechanical method
milestones.work: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola (letter to Dositheus)
milestones.description: Archimedes gives the area of a parabolic segment first by a lever argument and then by exhaustion.

evidence.claim: He first outlines the mechanical proof in Quadrature of the Parabola next to the geometric one, and gives a fuller account in The Method.
Heath's order places the Parabola before the Method.

milestones.note: Archimedes lived 287-212 BC and his works are undated, so the range is an outer bound. This work is also the first_application below.

milestones.label: Mechanical discovery of the parabola's area
milestones.work: Archimedes, Quadrature of the Parabola
milestones.description: The lever argument is used to find the area of a parabolic segment, later confirmed by exhaustion.

evidence.claim: Same source as above: the mechanical argument appears alongside the geometric proof.

milestones.note: Same work as the first_statement, listed twice because it carries both the statement and the first use.

milestones.label: The Method of Mechanical Theorems
milestones.work: Archimedes, Method concerning mechanical theorems, letter to Eratosthenes
milestones.description: Archimedes explains in a letter how balancing slices of figures led him to results such as sphere and cylinder volumes, which he then proved by exhaustion.

evidence.claim: It is a letter to Eratosthenes and holds the first attested explicit use of indivisibles.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, The Method of Mechanical Theorems

evidence.claim: Archimedes states that some results became clear by a mechanical method before geometric proof.
Heath's 1912 English edition (scanned).

milestones.label: Heiberg finds the Method in a palimpsest
milestones.work: J. L. Heiberg, discovery of the Archimedes Palimpsest, summer 1906
milestones.description: Heiberg recognised a tenth-century prayer book as carrying Archimedes' lost Method, so the text reached modern readers.

evidence.claim: In the summer of 1906 Heiberg discovered the manuscript that includes The Method.
The work was thought lost until its rediscovery in the palimpsest in 1906.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, The Method of Mechanical Theorems

milestones.note: Heiberg's 1907 publication in Hermes was not verified (not in Crossref).

milestones.label: Heath's English edition
milestones.work: T. L. Heath, The Method of Archimedes (Cambridge, 1912)
milestones.description: Heath's edition made the Method available in English with commentary.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive record of the 1912 edition.
evidence.source: Heath, The Method of Archimedes, recently discovered by Heiberg

milestones.label: Law of the lever and centres of gravity
milestones.work: Archimedes, On the Equilibrium of Planes
milestones.description: The mechanical method rests on the lever law and centres of gravity proved in this earlier treatise.

evidence.claim: The mechanical method relies on the centroid and lever law demonstrated in On the Equilibrium of Planes.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, The Method of Mechanical Theorems

milestones.note: Treatise undated; MacTutor follows Heath in placing it first among Archimedes' works but gives no year.

works.whyItMatters: Reconstructs the palimpsest that preserves Archimedes' Method, the source of his mechanical procedure.

works.citation: Discovery of the Method in the palimpsest
works.whyItMatters: Without this the method would be unknown.

works.citation: The Method of Archimedes, recently discovered by Heiberg
works.whyItMatters: First English edition and commentary.

notes: Dates of Archimedes' treatises are uncertain, so the first three milestones share the whole of his working life as a range. Archimedes did not count the method as a proof; he proved the same results by exhaustion (Wikipedia). Because the Method was lost until 1906, it had no direct influence on later calculus. No consolidation or naming milestone found; institutional date is null. Democritus' lifespan is from general knowledge. Netz and Noel, The Archimedes Codex (2007, Open Library OL16919237W) and the Palimpsest edition record the imaging; not used for a milestone. Searched: MacTutor Archimedes; Wikipedia Archimedes, The Method of Mechanical Theorems; Heath 1912 (Internet Archive); Crossref and zbMATH for Heiberg's 1907 paper (not found). person without verified work: Democritus (developer). Crossref search for Heiberg's 1907 Hermes article returned no match in this pass (only an 1884 Philologus article and an unrelated entry), so the 1907 date stays unverified; the 1906 discovery is the milestone date.

canonicalName: Babylonian astronomical parameters enter Greek astronomy

milestones.label: Meton's solstice and 19-year cycle
milestones.description: Meton's observation and cycle may reflect Babylonian period relations and were later used by Hipparchus and Ptolemy.

evidence.claim: Meton's observations proved very useful to later astronomers; it is unclear if the 19-year cycle was independent of Mesopotamia.
The Metonic and Saros relations may have come from Babylonian sources.

milestones.label: Hypsicles' 360-degree zodiac and arithmetic progressions
milestones.work: Hypsicles, On Ascensions (Anaphoricus)
milestones.description: Hypsicles divides the zodiac into 360 equal arcs and uses arithmetic progressions for rising times, a Babylonian-style scheme.

evidence.claim: He was the first to divide the zodiac into 360 degrees and used arithmetic progressions.
The division was probably introduced for all circles by Hypsicles, in Hipparchus' time.

milestones.note: Sources differ: Wikipedia also says Eudoxus and Timocharis already used 360 parts of the ecliptic. That the scheme is Babylonian is the usual view but was not checked in a primary study here.

milestones.label: Hipparchus adopts Babylonian lunar parameters
milestones.work: Hipparchus, lost treatises on lunar motion, reported in Ptolemy, Almagest IV
milestones.description: Hipparchus took Babylonian lunar period values as the basis for his Greek geometrical lunar model.

evidence.claim: For his lunar theory he needed mean motions and the best data were Babylonian parameters (Toomer quoted).
He seems the first to exploit Babylonian knowledge and techniques systematically.
Toomer's study of the lunar epicycle size.
evidence.source: Toomer, The size of the lunar epicycle according to Hipparchus, Centaurus 12 (1968)

milestones.note: Ptolemy attributes observations to Hipparchus from 147 to 127 BC (Wikipedia). His own texts are lost, so the earliest surviving report is Almagest IV.

milestones.label: Hipparchus tests the periods against eclipse records
milestones.work: Hipparchus, as described by Toomer and Ptolemy, Almagest IV.2
milestones.description: He built the eclipse period of 126,007 days 1 hour and checked it on eclipse pairs, using Babylonian records in a confirming role.

evidence.claim: Toomer says the observations confirmed rather than discovered the periods.
Toomer suggests Ptolemy's Babylonian eclipse data came from a list made by Hipparchus.

milestones.note: Same time range and same lost works as the previous milestone.

milestones.label: Ptolemy's Almagest absorbs Babylonian data
milestones.work: Ptolemy, Mathematike Syntaxis (Almagest), c. 150 AD
milestones.description: The Almagest preserves Hipparchus' use of Babylonian periods and eclipse records and fixes them in the standard Greek models.

evidence.claim: Kugler showed Almagest IV.2 reports periods that Hipparchus confirmed from Babylonian ephemerides.
Ptolemy's knowledge of Babylonian eclipse records may come from Hipparchus.
Date of the Almagest.

milestones.label: Kugler identifies Hipparchus' Babylonian periods
milestones.work: F. X. Kugler, Die babylonische Mondrechnung (Freiburg, 1900)
milestones.description: Kugler found that the lunar periods Ptolemy credits to Hipparchus already appear in Babylonian System B texts.

evidence.claim: In 1900 Kugler showed that Hipparchus' periods had already been used in Babylonian ephemerides.
Scanned copy of the book.

milestones.label: Neugebauer's History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy
milestones.work: O. Neugebauer, A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy (Springer, 1975)
milestones.description: Neugebauer gives the standard systematic account of Babylonian astronomy and its transmission to Greek astronomy.

evidence.claim: Open Library record, 1975.
evidence.source: Neugebauer, A history of ancient mathematical astronomy

evidence.claim: Chapter on Babylonian astronomy in the same volume series.

works.citation: Toomer, Hipparchus on the distances of the sun and moon, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 14
works.whyItMatters: Modern reconstruction of one of his lost works.
Standard English translation of the Almagest, including its chord and trigonometric material.
Showed the Babylonian origin of the lunar periods.

works.citation: A history of ancient mathematical astronomy
works.whyItMatters: Standard account.

works.citation: Hipparchus and Babylonian astronomy, in Studies in Memory of Abraham Sachs
works.whyItMatters: Key study of the contact; listed in Wikipedia's bibliography, no library record checked.

notes: The direction and date of transmission are partly open: Wikipedia notes the only securely dated tablet with Hipparchus' long lunar period is later than him, so tablets do not settle priority. Whether Hipparchus visited Babylon is unknown. All first-century and earlier Greek evidence is second-hand through Ptolemy. First_statement and first_application share the same lost works. Searched: MacTutor Hipparchus, Hypsicles, Greek astronomy; Wikipedia Hipparchus, Babylonian astronomy, Almagest; Crossref and zbMATH for Toomer; Internet Archive for Kugler. person without verified work: Hypsicles (developer).

canonicalName: Trigonometry from astronomy: Hipparchus and chord tables

milestones.label: Greek spherical geometry for astronomy
milestones.work: Autolycus, On the Moving Sphere, c. 330 BC
milestones.description: Autolycus wrote the earliest surviving text on spherical geometry for astronomy, without trigonometry.

evidence.claim: A key text on spherical geometry was written by Autolycus in Athens around 330 BC.
Theodosius' Sphaerics, c. 100 BC, has no trigonometry.

milestones.label: Hipparchus' table of chords
milestones.work: Hipparchus, twelve books on chords (lost), c. 140 BC
milestones.description: Hipparchus tabulated chord lengths against arcs so that triangles could be solved, usually counted as the start of trigonometry.

evidence.claim: The first known table of chords is by Hipparchus about 140 BC; the books are lost.
He is the first mathematician known to have a trigonometric table; Theon names the work.
Standard study.
evidence.source: Toomer, The chord table of Hipparchus and the early history of Greek trigonometry, Centaurus 18 (1974)

milestones.note: Neither table survives; Ptolemy's relation to it is uncertain (Wikipedia). MacTutor says the claim of twelve books is a claim.

milestones.label: Chords used to compute eccentricities
milestones.work: Hipparchus (lost works, via Ptolemy)
milestones.description: Hipparchus needed the table to compute the eccentricity of the Moon's and Sun's orbits.

evidence.claim: He needed the table when computing eccentricities of lunar and solar orbits.
The purpose of the table was a method for solving triangles without starting from first principles.

milestones.note: Same lost works as the first_statement.

milestones.label: Menelaus' Sphaerica
milestones.work: Menelaus of Alexandria, Sphaerica, c. 100 AD
milestones.description: Menelaus proves the theorem on the sphere now named after him, the earliest surviving work on spherical trigonometry.

evidence.claim: Menelaus' work on spherics is the earliest known work on spherical trigonometry.
Book III contains Menelaus' theorem.

milestones.label: Ptolemy's chord table and addition formulas
milestones.work: Ptolemy, Almagest I.10-11, c. 150 AD
milestones.description: Ptolemy builds a chord table at half-degree steps and proves sum, difference and half-angle rules, the first surviving systematic trigonometry.

evidence.claim: He derived addition formulas from his theorem and computed chords by inscribed polygons and half-arc rules.
The table is in Book I, chapter 11 of the Almagest and is the earliest extensive trigonometric table.
Standard English translation.

milestones.label: Aryabhata's table of half-chords
milestones.work: Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya, 499 AD
milestones.description: Aryabhata gives a table of half-chords, effectively the first sine table, using the word jya.

evidence.claim: Around 500 Aryabhata gave tables of half-chords which are sine tables.
He finished the Aryabhatiya in 499 at age 23.
The idea of Greek descent for the table has been refuted; scholars argue for an independent origin.

milestones.note: Wikipedia and MacTutor differ on the amount of Greek influence.

milestones.label: Al-Tusi's Treatise on the Quadrilateral
milestones.work: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Treatise on the Quadrilateral
milestones.description: Al-Tusi treats plane and spherical trigonometry as a subject of its own, apart from astronomy.

evidence.claim: It is described as the first work treating trigonometry as an independent branch of pure mathematics.
Wikipedia gives the same assessment and notes European credit often went to Regiomontanus.

milestones.note: MacTutor gives no date for the treatise; al-Tusi died in 1274 and the Maragheh observatory started in 1259. Regiomontanus' De triangulis omnimodis (1464) is the parallel Latin systematic treatise.

milestones.label: Pitiscus' Trigonometria
milestones.work: Bartholomaeus Pitiscus, Trigonometria, in Scultetus, Sphaericorum libri tres (Heidelberg, 1595)
milestones.description: The word trigonometry first appears in the title of Pitiscus' tract, printed with Scultetus' book on the sphere.

evidence.claim: The word is due to Pitiscus and first occurs in this 1595 title.
Scanned 1595 volume with the appended treatise on solving triangles.
Same date in the general history.

works.citation: Toomer, The chord table of Hipparchus, Centaurus 18
works.whyItMatters: Main modern analysis.
Modern critical edition of Menelaus' spherical trigonometry.
Standard English translation of the Almagest, including its chord and trigonometric material.
First surviving sine table.
Gave the field its name.

notes: This event bundles several phases; later phases (Indian sine, Islamic trigonometry) are shown only as milestones. Hipparchus' table is lost, and some scholars date or credit the earliest chord tables differently (Toomer's own doubts are noted on Wikipedia). Whether Hipparchus invented trigonometry is a matter of definition. Regiomontanus, De triangulis omnimodis (1464, MacTutor) is a further consolidation not listed. Van Brummelen (2009, Open Library OL12006672W) is a modern survey. Searched: MacTutor Trigonometric functions, Hipparchus, Menelaus, Ptolemy, Pitiscus, Aryabhata, Al-Tusi; Wikipedia History of trigonometry, Hipparchus, Ptolemy's table of chords; Crossref and zbMATH. person without verified work: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (systematiser).

milestones.label: Autolycus' On the Moving Sphere
milestones.work: Autolycus of Pitane, On the Moving Sphere
milestones.description: Autolycus supplied early theorems on the rotating sphere used in astronomy.

evidence.claim: An important text on spherical geometry was written by Autolycus around 330 BC.

milestones.label: Theodosius' Sphaerics
milestones.work: Theodosius, Sphaerics, c. 100 BC
milestones.description: Theodosius gives the geometry of the sphere as a supplement to Euclid, with no trigonometry.

evidence.claim: Sphaerics contains no trigonometry and was written to supplement Euclid with sphere geometry; Theodosius lived close to 100 BC.
Menelaus' Book 2 largely follows Theodosius' propositions with better proofs.

milestones.label: Menelaus defines the spherical triangle and proves his theorem
milestones.work: Menelaus of Alexandria, Sphaerica, Book I and III.1
milestones.description: Menelaus defines the spherical triangle and proves the collinearity theorem on the sphere, now named after him.

evidence.claim: He gave the first definition of a spherical triangle, and Book III opens with Menelaus' theorem.
Wikipedia notes he named the figures trilaterals and proved the theorem.

milestones.note: Menelaus' observations in Rome in January 98 are cited in Almagest VII.3; Sphaerica itself is undated, so the range runs from 98 to his approximate death in 130.

milestones.label: Euclid-style treatment of spherical triangles
milestones.work: Menelaus of Alexandria, Sphaerica, Book I
milestones.description: Book I builds spherical triangles in the way Euclid builds plane triangles, in some respects more completely.

evidence.claim: He set up the basis for treating spherical triangles as Euclid treated plane ones.

milestones.note: Same work as the first_statement.

milestones.label: Spherical geometry applied to astronomy
milestones.work: Menelaus of Alexandria, Sphaerica, Book II
milestones.description: Book II applies the spherical theorems to astronomical problems.

evidence.claim: Book 2 applies spherical geometry to astronomy.

milestones.note: Same work again; the three roles are distinct books of one treatise.

milestones.label: Arabic translations and revisions of Sphaerica
milestones.work: Arabic versions (including Ibn Iraq, al-Mahani, al-Harawi)
milestones.description: The Greek text is lost; Sphaerica survives through several Arabic versions, which differ and were studied by al-Tusi and others.

evidence.claim: Many Arabic translations and commentaries exist and make reconstruction hard.
Edition of the early translation and the al-Mahani/al-Harawi version.
evidence.source: Rashed and Papadopoulos, Menelaus' Spherics (De Gruyter, 2017)

evidence.claim: Study of Ibn Iraq's treatment of Spherics III.5.
evidence.source: Rashed and Papadopoulos, Arabic Sciences and Philosophy (2014)

milestones.note: Century range from the persons named in the record titles; individual translators' dates were not checked.

milestones.label: Halley's printed edition
milestones.work: E. Halley, Menelai Sphaericorum libri III (Oxford, 1758)
milestones.description: Halley's edition, built from Hebrew and Arabic manuscripts, first printed the work in the West.

evidence.claim: Open Library records an edition dated 1758.
Internet Archive record naming Halley and Costard.

milestones.note: The claim that it was the first Western print rests on general knowledge; the records only show a 1758 edition.

milestones.label: Modern critical edition
milestones.work: Rashed and Papadopoulos, Menelaus' Spherics (2017)
milestones.description: A scholarly edition with translation of the Arabic versions replaced earlier partial editions.

evidence.claim: Crossref and zbMATH record for the 2017 volume.
evidence.source: Menelaus' Spherics: Early Translation and al-Mahani/al-Harawi's Version

works.whyItMatters: Modern critical edition of Menelaus' spherical trigonometry.
Standard English translation of the Almagest, including its chord and trigonometric material.
Modern critical edition.

works.citation: Autolycus of Pitane, On the Moving Sphere (Autolyci De sphaera quae movetur liber), edited by Friedrich Hultsch, 1885 (original c. 330 BC, approximate)
works.whyItMatters: Greek text on the geometry of the rotating sphere, the background that Menelaus' Sphaerica extends to spherical triangles.

works.citation: Theodosius of Bithynia, Sphaerica (original c. 100 BCE per the record); edition catalogued as 'Sphaerica' (1927), Open Library
works.whyItMatters: Theodosius' Sphaerics is the pre-Menelaus treatise of spherical geometry that the record places before Menelaus' Sphaerica.

notes: The plane form of the theorem was known before Menelaus (MacTutor), and some historians think Hipparchus already solved spherical triangles (MacTutor, Theodosius), so Menelaus is better called the earliest surviving source. Sphaerica is undated; the milestones use the range 98-130 and the three roles all refer to the same treatise. Rashed's birth year is from general knowledge and was not verified. Searched: MacTutor Menelaus, Theodosius, Greek astronomy; Wikipedia Menelaus of Alexandria; Crossref, zbMATH and Open Library for editions. person without verified work: Theodosius of Bithynia (developer). person without verified work: Autolycus of Pitane (developer).

milestones.label: Hipparchus' chord tables and solar and lunar models
milestones.description: Hipparchus supplied the chord table, the solar eccentric model and a lunar epicycle model that the Almagest builds on.

evidence.claim: The Syntaxis adopted Hipparchus' solar model; he made models for Sun and Moon but not the planets.
Most of what is known about Hipparchus comes from the Almagest.

milestones.label: Canopic Inscription
milestones.work: Ptolemy, inscription at Canopus, 147 or 148 AD
milestones.description: A public inscription gives an earlier version of Ptolemy's models, so the Almagest is later than it.

evidence.claim: Hamilton found that the models in the inscription are earlier than those in the Almagest, so the Almagest dates from about 150 or after.

milestones.label: The Almagest (Mathematike Syntaxis)
milestones.work: Ptolemy, Mathematike Syntaxis, c. 150 AD
milestones.description: Ptolemy's thirteen books give the mathematical theory of the Sun, Moon and planets, with chord trigonometry in Book I.

evidence.claim: Written possibly around 150, in thirteen books; Book I has the chord table.
It is a treatise in thirteen books; the first two present the trigonometric tools.
Standard English translation.

milestones.note: No fixed publication year; dated by the Canopic Inscription and the text's contents.

milestones.label: Chord trigonometry applied to the planets
milestones.work: Ptolemy, Almagest, Books II-XIII
milestones.description: Ptolemy uses the chord function and spherical methods throughout to compute the motions of Sun, Moon and planets, and adds the equant for the planets.

evidence.claim: He introduces the equant and succeeds in modelling the planets where Hipparchus did not.
He first sets out the mathematics needed, then applies it to the Sun and Moon.

milestones.note: Same work as the first_statement.

milestones.label: Arabic translations
milestones.work: Arabic Almagest (9th century)
milestones.description: Arabic scholars began translating the work in the ninth century; the oldest surviving copies are from then.

evidence.claim: The text survives in copies; Arabic scholars began to translate it in the 9th century.

milestones.label: Almagestum: the name from Arabic al-majisti
milestones.work: Gerard of Cremona, Latin translation from Arabic (finished 1175)
milestones.description: The name Almagest comes from the Arabic form of the Greek superlative and was spread by Gerard's Latin version.

evidence.claim: The name was popularised by the Latin Almagestum of the 12th century; Gerard finished in 1175.
MacTutor explains the chain from Mathematike Syntaxis to Almagest.

milestones.note: Names the book, not a field.

milestones.label: Regiomontanus' Epitome of the Almagest printed
milestones.work: Regiomontanus, Epytoma in Almagestum Ptolemaei, printed 1496 (completed in manuscript 1462)
milestones.description: Regiomontanus condensed the Almagest into a guide that was printed in 1496; it was completed in manuscript in 1462.

evidence.claim: He completed the Epitome in 1462.
Open Library dates the printed Epytoma to 1496.
Open Library lists Epytoma in Almagestum Ptolemaei with first publication year 1496

milestones.label: Toomer's English translation
milestones.work: G. J. Toomer, Ptolemy's Almagest (Springer, 1984)
milestones.description: Toomer's annotated translation from the Greek became the standard modern text.

evidence.claim: Springer 1984 listed in zbMATH; Wikipedia names it as the second English translation.
Open Library record of the work.

works.whyItMatters: Standard English translation of the Almagest, including its chord and trigonometric material.

works.citation: Toomer, Hipparchus on the distances of the sun and moon, Arch. Hist. Exact Sci. 14 (1974)
works.whyItMatters: Modern reconstruction of one of Hipparchus' lost works, which used the Babylonian parameters.
Gave the text and name to Latin Europe.
Compendium and defence of Ptolemy.
Standard English translation.

notes: The Almagest has no publication year; c. 150 follows the Canopic Inscription argument (Hamilton). The star catalogue may partly come from Hipparchus (Wikipedia). Newton's charges of fraud are rejected by Gingerich. Heiberg's Greek edition and the Basel editio princeps (1538) were not verified. Gerard's lifespan is from general knowledge. The chord table itself (I.11) is also covered in event H75.
